newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FOCUS-Romania rushes privatisation for IMF review.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Romania rushes privatisation for IMF review.

text.p: Romania, faced with an IMF review of its performance this month, announced ambitious plans on Friday to step up privatisation, a key element of its accords with international lenders.

State Ownership Fund (FPS) President Sorin Dimitriu said his agency, which is subordinated to the government, would turn a bank over to the private sector this year and float dozens of companies on the capital market.
"We will privatise Banca Romana pentru Dezvoltare (BRD) by the end of the year," Dimitriu told a news conference. "Also this year, we will start preparing the selloff of Banc Post."

In a separate interview, Dimitriu said the FPS, which has controlling interests in most Romanian companies, was preparing to sell stakes in 60 companies on the Bucharest stock exchange next month. A further five would go into private hands on the over-the-counter market in two months' time.

The government scored further points on Friday when a decree on foreign investment won parliamentary approval. The decree amends and complements a 1991 law on foreign inflows, granting incentives to direct and portfolio investors.

The centrist coalition, which came to power in elections last November after seven years of sluggish reforms under ex-communists, has promised rapid change. Heading the list of priorities are faster privatisation and restructuring of communist-era, loss-making industrial giants.

Its programme quickly won the support of international lenders, with the International Monetary Fund approving a stand-by credit of $430 million and the World Bank agreeing to disburse loans of over $700 million.

An IMF mission to review progress in implementing reforms is expected in Bucharest this month. The review is due to be formally concluded in September or October, when the Fund will set benchmarks for the second half of 1997.
The IMF's resident representative gave the government programme a ringing endorsement last month, saying reform measures were bearing fruit and deserved international support.
He cited a fall in monthly inflation to 4.3 percent in May from more than 30 percent in March after price liberalisation, as well as a rise in central bank foreign reserves.
Monthly inflation is targeted to fall to two percent by the end of the year and the budget deficit is to be trimmed to 4.5 percent of gross domestic product from last year's 5.8 percent.

Privatisation, launched two years after Romania shed communism in 1989, made slow progress under leftist rule. Only about 3,000 of more than 6,500 targeted state enterprises had been sold off by the end of last year.
Bank stake sales would be aimed at strategic foreign investors, Dimitriu said. "For banks, we need banking investors recognised in the international banking community."
Privatisation of state banks, another benchmark of Romania's loan accords, was given the go-ahead earlier this year when a bank selloff bill cleared parliament.
The banking sector, one of the fastest growing in post-communist Romania, is made up of 42 commercial banks. No bank has been declared bankrupt so far.
Dimitriu said Western and local banks had shown interest in buying stakes in Romanian banks, but gave no names.

Other steps to increase the pace of selloffs included a public share offer for four companies expected early next month, and sales of majority stakes in pharmaceutical companies and of smaller share packages in some of the already listed stocks.
Romania operates a stock exchange in Bucharest which trades 46 companies, as well as an over-the-counter market, where the number of listings stands at more than 3,000.
